The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(v_p(n)\) denote the exponent of a prime \(p\) in \(n\).

For a move replacing \(a,b\) by \(\gcd(a,b),\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\), each prime exponent pair \((v_p(a),v_p(b))\) is replaced by
\[
\min(v_p(a),v_p(b)),\quad \max(v_p(a),v_p(b)).
\]
So for every prime \(p\), the multiset of \(p\)-adic exponents on the board is invariant.

At the stopping time, no move changes the board. This means every pair of numbers on the board is comparable by divisibility; otherwise replacing an incomparable pair would change the board. Thus the final \(2100\) numbers form a chain under divisibility.

Arrange the final numbers in increasing order:
\[
x_1\le x_2\le \cdots \le x_{2100}.
\]
Since they form a divisibility chain, \(x_i\mid x_j\) for \(i<j\). Therefore, for each prime \(p\), the sequence
\[
v_p(x_1),v_p(x_2),\dots,v_p(x_{2100})
\]
is nondecreasing. Its multiset is exactly the multiset of \(p\)-adic exponents of \(1,2,\dots,2100\). Hence \(v_p(x_i)\) is the \(i\)-th smallest value among the \(p\)-adic exponents of \(1,2,\dots,2100\).

So the desired number is \(x_{2026}\). For a fixed prime \(p\), let
\[
c_p=v_p(x_{2026}).
\]
The \(2026\)-th smallest of \(2100\) values is the largest \(t\) such that at least
\[
2100-2026+1=75
\]
of the numbers \(1,2,\dots,2100\) have \(p\)-adic exponent at least \(t\). The number of such integers is
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus
\[
c_p=\max\left\{t:\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor\ge 75\right\}.
\]

Now compute:

- For \(p=2\):
  \[
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{2^4}\right\rfloor=131\ge75,\qquad
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{2^5}\right\rfloor=65<75,
  \]
  so \(c_2=4\).

- For \(p=3\):
  \[
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{3^3}\right\rfloor=77\ge75,\qquad
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{3^4}\right\rfloor=25<75,
  \]
  so \(c_3=3\).

- For \(p=5\):
  \[
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{5^2}\right\rfloor=84\ge75,\qquad
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{5^3}\right\rfloor=16<75,
  \]
  so \(c_5=2\).

- For \(p=7,11,13,17,19,23\), we have
  \[
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{p}\right\rfloor\ge75,\qquad
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{p^2}\right\rfloor<75,
  \]
  so \(c_p=1\).

- For every prime \(p\ge29\),
  \[
  \left\lfloor\frac{2100}{p}\right\rfloor\le 72<75,
  \]
  so \(c_p=0\).

Therefore,
\[
x_{2026}=2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]
The number of positive divisors is
\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot64
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
